DE-A2-01-001.notes: weil is a subordinating conjunction, so the conjugated verb goes to the very end: weil ich in Berlin arbeite. A comma always separates the subordinate clause.

DE-A2-01-002.notes: After weil, the verb bin moves behind krank to the end of the clause. In casual speech you'll hear weil + main-clause order (weil ich bin krank), but it's avoided in writing.

DE-A2-01-003.notes: dass sends the verb to the end: dass er keine Zeit hat. In speech, dass can be dropped after sagen, and then main-clause order returns: Er sagt, er hat keine Zeit.

DE-A2-01-004.notes: dass (that) introduces a statement and is spelt with ss; das (the, that) is an article or pronoun. The verb regnet goes to the end of the dass-clause.

DE-A2-01-005.notes: ob means 'whether' and turns a yes/no question into an indirect one: Kommt er? → ob er kommt. Using wenn here is a common English-based error.

DE-A2-01-006.notes: In an indirect question with wann, the verb goes to the end, and a separable verb rejoins its prefix: wann der Zug ankommt, not kommt … an.

DE-A2-01-007.notes: With a modal in a subordinate clause, the modal comes last, after the infinitive: dass du gut kochen kannst.

DE-A2-01-008.notes: When the wenn-clause comes first, it fills position one, so the main clause begins with its verb: Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir… The two verbs meet at the comma.

DE-A2-01-009.notes: als is for a single event or period in the past (als ich 18 war); wenn is for the present, the future or repeated events (whenever). English 'when' covers both.
DE-A2-01-009.tip: als: one occasion in the past; wenn: whenever.

DE-A2-01-010.notes: weil sends the verb to the end; denn keeps normal word order (denn ich bin krank) and can't begin a sentence. Both give a reason.

DE-A2-02-001.notes: gehen in den Park is movement towards a destination (wohin?), so the two-way preposition in takes the accusative: den Park.

DE-A2-02-002.notes: spielen im Park is location (wo?), so in takes the dative: in dem → im. The contraction im is almost always used.

DE-A2-02-003.notes: legen is a verb of putting, so auf takes the accusative: auf den Tisch. legen is used for putting something flat.

DE-A2-02-004.notes: liegen describes position, so auf takes the dative: auf dem Tisch. The verb pair legen / liegen mirrors the accusative / dative pair.

DE-A2-02-005.notes: hängen with an object (I hang it) is movement to a place, so an takes the accusative: an die Wand. an is used for vertical surfaces.

DE-A2-02-006.notes: hängen without an object (it hangs) is position, so an takes the dative: an der Wand. Feminine die changes to der in the dative.

DE-A2-02-007.notes: fahren ans Meer is movement, so an + das contracts to ans. ans Meer (to the seaside) uses an because the sea is a boundary you go up to.

DE-A2-02-008.notes: sein am Meer is location, so an + dem contracts to am. The same phrase gives am See, am Fluss. For a lake or river by name, the same an applies: am Rhein.

DE-A2-02-009.notes: schlafen unter dem Bett is location, so unter takes the dative: dem Bett. Bett is neuter, so das → dem.

DE-A2-02-010.notes: springen auf das Sofa is movement onto it, so auf takes the accusative: das Sofa. The neuter accusative looks the same as the nominative.

DE-A2-02-011.notes: her marks movement towards the speaker, hin away from the speaker. They combine with prefixes and question words: herein, hinaus, woher, wohin.
DE-A2-02-011.tip: her = towards me; hin = away from me.

DE-A2-02-012.notes: stellen (put upright) is a regular verb of putting and takes the accusative; stehen (be standing) is irregular and takes the dative. Bottles stand, so stellen / stehen.

DE-A2-02-013.notes: legen (put flat) takes the accusative: aufs Bett. liegen (be lying) takes the dative: auf dem Bett. A phone lies flat, so legen / liegen.

DE-A2-02-014.notes: sich setzen (sit down) is the movement, with the accusative: aufs Sofa. sitzen (be sitting) is the position, with the dative: auf dem Sofa.

DE-A2-02-015.notes: hängen as 'hang something up' is regular: hängte, gehängt. an den Haken is accusative because it's movement to a place.
DE-A2-02-015.text: Ich habe den Mantel an den Haken {{c1::gehängt::hängen (put up) · past participle}}.
DE-A2-02-015.tr: I hung my coat on the hook.
DE-A2-02-015.flag: dup: replaced Ich habe das Bild an die Wand gehängt (near-identical to A2-02-005)

DE-A2-02-016.notes: hängen as 'be hanging' is irregular: hing, gehangen. Das Bild hat … gehangen describes a state that lasted, so it takes haben.

DE-A2-02-017.notes: Events take auf + accusative for 'going to': auf eine Party, auf ein Konzert. Being there is auf + dative: auf der Party.

DE-A2-02-018.notes: Shops, services and institutions take zu: zu der Post → zur Post. noch müssen = still have to (go somewhere); the verb gehen is often left out.

DE-A2-02-019.notes: Universities take an + dative for 'at': an der Uni Heidelberg. Schools are different: an der Schule or in der Schule.

DE-A2-02-020.notes: Markets take auf + dative: auf dem Markt. Going there is auf + accusative: auf den Markt gehen. Shops and buildings take in instead: im Supermarkt.

DE-A2-02-021.notes: bei + workplace or activity means 'at': bei der Arbeit, bei der Post (working there). bei always takes the dative.

DE-A2-02-022.notes: Being at the doctor's is bei + dative: bei dem → beim Arzt. Going there is zum Arzt. Likewise beim Friseur, beim Zahnarzt.

DE-A2-02-023.notes: bei + people means 'at their place': wohnen bei meinen Eltern. mit means 'together with': ins Kino gehen mit meinen Eltern. Both take the dative.

DE-A2-03-001.notes: schenken takes the person in the dative and the gift in the accusative: meiner Mutter (dative) Blumen (accusative). Two nouns: dative first.

DE-A2-03-002.notes: zeigen takes a dative person, and the dative plural article is den with -n on the noun: den Kindern. die Stadt is the accusative thing shown.

DE-A2-03-003.notes: gehören (belong to) takes the dative: meinem Vater. The thing owned is the subject, so gehört agrees with das Auto.

DE-A2-03-004.notes: schmecken takes the dative of the person tasting: dir. Wie schmeckt dir das Essen? is the standard question about food; the subject is das Essen.

DE-A2-03-005.notes: passen (fit, suit) takes the dative: mir. The clothing is the subject, so passt agrees with die Hose, which is singular in German.

DE-A2-03-006.notes: danken takes the dative: Ihnen, with a capital for formal Sie. The reason follows with für + accusative: für Ihre Hilfe.

DE-A2-03-007.notes: gefallen takes the dative of the person: Ihnen, the formal dative, always capitalised. The verb agrees with das Hotel.

DE-A2-03-008.notes: With two pronouns, the accusative comes before the dative: es ihm. With two nouns, the order is reversed: dem Mann das Buch.

DE-A2-03-009.notes: fragen takes the accusative, even though English might suggest 'ask to': Ich frage den Lehrer. The question itself can follow with nach + dative.

DE-A2-03-010.notes: gratulieren takes the dative: dir. Ich gratuliere dir is a complete congratulation; zum Geburtstag can be added with zu + dative.

DE-A2-03-011.notes: glauben takes the dative of a person (believe someone): ihm. A thing believed is accusative: Ich glaube das nicht. glauben an + accusative means believe in.

DE-A2-03-012.notes: anrufen takes the accusative, unlike English 'call to': mich. In a du imperative, the prefix an still goes to the end.

DE-A2-03-013.notes: folgen takes the dative: mir. It forms the Perfekt with sein when it means following physically: Er ist mir gefolgt.

DE-A2-03-014.notes: gefallen makes the thing liked the subject and suits impressions (a film); mögen + noun states a general liking (cheese); gern + verb means liking an activity.

DE-A2-03-015.notes: Physical sensations use a dative pronoun with ist + adjective: Mir ist kalt. Ich bin kalt would describe a cold personality.
DE-A2-03-015.tip: Mir ist kalt, not Ich bin kalt.

DE-A2-03-016.notes: Boredom works the same way: Ist dir langweilig? Du bist langweilig would mean you are boring. The answer might be Nein, mir ist nicht langweilig.

DE-A2-03-017.notes: Ihm ist schlecht means he feels sick, with er in the dative. Er ist schlecht would mean he's bad (at something, or morally).

DE-A2-04-001.notes: After der (definite article), the adjective in the masculine nominative takes -e: der neue Lehrer. The article already shows the gender and case.

DE-A2-04-002.notes: After den (masculine accusative), the adjective takes -en: den roten Pullover. -en appears everywhere after der-words except the five -e positions.

DE-A2-04-003.notes: Feminine nominative after die takes -e: die kleine Katze. The feminine accusative is the same: Ich sehe die kleine Katze.

DE-A2-04-004.notes: Neuter nominative after das takes -e: das alte Haus. Neuter accusative is identical, so das alte Haus covers both cases.

DE-A2-04-005.notes: All dative forms after a der-word take -en: mit dem neuen Auto. mit always triggers the dative. mit dem Auto fahren itself means 'go by car'.

DE-A2-04-006.notes: Plural adjectives after die take -en: die jungen Leute. Only the singular nominative and feminine / neuter accusative take -e.

DE-A2-04-007.notes: ein shows no gender in the masculine nominative, so the adjective does: ein guter Film (-er, like der). After der it would be der gute Film.

DE-A2-04-008.notes: ein shows no gender in the neuter nominative or accusative, so the adjective takes -es, like das: ein schönes Kleid.

DE-A2-04-009.notes: eine already shows feminine, so the adjective takes -e: eine große Wohnung. The pattern after eine matches the one after die.

DE-A2-04-010.notes: einen shows masculine accusative, so the adjective takes -en: einen billigen Laptop. Every masculine accusative adjective ends in -en.

DE-A2-04-011.notes: einem shows the dative, so the adjective takes -en: in einem kleinen Dorf. in + dative because wohnen describes location.

DE-A2-04-012.notes: With no article, the adjective takes the der-word ending itself: den → kalten Kaffee (masculine accusative -en).

DE-A2-04-013.notes: No article, neuter nominative, so the adjective takes the das ending -es: frisches Brot. It does the article's job of showing case and gender.

DE-A2-04-014.notes: After sein, werden or bleiben, adjectives take no ending: Der Film ist gut. Endings only appear before a noun.

DE-A2-04-015.notes: With no article, the adjective takes the dative ending of dem itself: großem Interesse (-em). Set phrases like mit großem Interesse and bei schönem Wetter are common.

DE-A2-05-001.notes: The comparative adds -er, and many one-syllable adjectives add an umlaut: groß → größer. than is als, never wie.

DE-A2-05-002.notes: alt → älter, with umlaut. After als, the standard pronoun is nominative: älter als ich, matching English 'than I'.

DE-A2-05-003.notes: warm → wärmer. With es and the weather, comparatives work as in English: Heute ist es wärmer als gestern.

DE-A2-05-004.notes: gut has an irregular comparative: besser. The superlative is am besten or der / die / das beste. Before a noun it declines: ein besserer Plan.

DE-A2-05-005.notes: viel → mehr, which never takes an ending: mehr Geld, mehr Leute. weniger (less, fewer) works the same way.

DE-A2-05-006.notes: gern → lieber → am liebsten. Ich esse am liebsten Pizza is the natural way to name a favourite; favourite as a noun is Lieblings-: mein Lieblingsessen.

DE-A2-05-007.notes: hoch → höher → der höchste. Before a noun, the superlative takes adjective endings: der höchste Berg (-e after der).

DE-A2-05-008.notes: After a verb, the superlative takes am + -sten: am kältesten. Adjectives in -t add -e- before -sten for pronunciation.

DE-A2-05-009.notes: A comparative takes als (than); equality takes so … wie (as … as). größer wie is colloquial and non-standard.

DE-A2-06-001.notes: sich freuen auf + accusative = look forward to. The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: ich freue mich.

DE-A2-06-002.notes: sich kennenlernen with a plural subject means 'meet each other, get to know each other': wir haben uns kennengelernt. The reflexive uns is the reciprocal 'each other'.
DE-A2-06-002.text: Wir haben {{c1::uns::reflexive · wir}} im Urlaub kennengelernt.
DE-A2-06-002.flag: dup: replaced Wir treffen uns um acht (near-identical to A1-10-001 Wir treffen uns am Freitag um acht Uhr)

DE-A2-06-003.notes: sich interessieren für + accusative = be interested in. du takes the reflexive dich. The question about the thing is Wofür interessierst du dich?

DE-A2-06-004.notes: sich waschen changes a → ä in the er form: er wäscht sich. The third-person reflexive is always sich.

DE-A2-06-005.notes: With another object (die Zähne), the reflexive becomes dative: mir. German uses the reflexive dative instead of a possessive: not meine Zähne.

DE-A2-06-006.notes: The formal reflexive is sich, lower-case, even though Sie is capitalised. Setzen Sie sich is a polite invitation to sit.

DE-A2-06-007.notes: With no other object, the reflexive is accusative: mich. With a body part as object, it becomes dative: mir die Hände.

DE-A2-07-001.notes: trinken has the irregular participle getrunken, with i → u. Strong verbs often change their vowel in the participle and end in -en.

DE-A2-07-002.notes: schreiben → geschrieben, with ei → ie. The dative mir (to me) comes before the accusative eine E-Mail.

DE-A2-07-003.notes: finden → gefunden, with i → u. The participle goes to the end of the question: Hast du … gefunden? The Präteritum is fand: Ich fand den Schlüssel nicht.

DE-A2-07-004.notes: schlafen → geschlafen, with no vowel change; the a → ä of the present (er schläft) doesn't carry over. lange schlafen = sleep in. The Präteritum is schlief.

DE-A2-07-005.notes: nehmen → genommen, with e → o and a doubled m. den Zug nehmen = take the train. The Präteritum is nahm, with a long a.

DE-A2-07-006.notes: sein has the participle gewesen and forms the Perfekt with sein: Ich bin gewesen. noch nie = never (yet).

DE-A2-07-007.notes: Verbs with the inseparable prefix be- take no ge-: besucht. The other inseparable prefixes are ver-, er-, ent-, emp-, ge-, zer-.

DE-A2-07-008.notes: verstehen has the prefix ver- and an irregular stem: verstanden, with no ge-. The negation nicht goes before the participle.

DE-A2-07-009.notes: erklären has the inseparable prefix er-, so no ge-: erklärt. It's otherwise regular, ending in -t. Its noun is die Erklärung (explanation).

DE-A2-07-010.notes: passieren ends in -ieren, so no ge-: passiert. It forms the Perfekt with sein, because something comes about.

DE-A2-07-011.notes: aufstehen is separable and irregular: auf-ge-standen. It takes sein, as a change of position. In the present it splits: Ich stehe um sechs auf.

DE-A2-07-012.notes: umziehen (move house) is separable: um-ge-zogen, with sein. sich umziehen means 'get changed' and takes haben.

DE-A2-07-013.notes: denken is a mixed verb: vowel change plus -t, gedacht. denken an + accusative = think of; daran refers back to a thing or idea.
DE-A2-07-013.text: Daran habe ich nicht {{c1::gedacht::denken · past participle}}.
DE-A2-07-013.flag: dup: replaced Ich habe oft an dich gedacht (near-identical to B1-01-002 Ich denke oft an dich)

DE-A2-07-014.notes: mitbringen is separable and mixed: mit-ge-bracht. bringen changes to brach- plus -t in the participle.

DE-A2-07-015.notes: wissen is mixed: gewusst, with i → u and -t. Hast du das gewusst? is the natural spoken past; Wusstest du das? is equally common.

DE-A2-07-016.notes: nennen is mixed: genannt, with e → a. nennen means 'name, call'; heißen is used for what someone is called.

DE-A2-07-017.notes: rennen is mixed: gerannt, and takes sein as a verb of movement. zum Bus rennen = run for the bus. Its Präteritum, rannte, is also mixed.

DE-A2-08-001.notes: Modals in the past normally use the Präteritum: ich konnte. The umlaut of können disappears: konnte, not könnte (which means could, hypothetically).

DE-A2-08-002.notes: müssen → mussten, without the umlaut. The Perfekt (haben warten müssen) exists but is much rarer. lange warten = wait a long time.

DE-A2-08-003.notes: wollen → wollte. The ich and er forms have no extra ending: er wollte. werden after wollen is an infinitive at the end.

DE-A2-08-004.notes: dürfen → durfte, without the umlaut. Als Kind takes first position, so the verb durfte comes second.

DE-A2-08-005.notes: es gibt has the past es gab, used in speech as well as writing. Früher = in the past, it used to be.

DE-A2-08-006.notes: wissen → wusste, with i → u and -te. Ich wusste das nicht = I didn't know that. The Konjunktiv II is wüsste (would know).

DE-A2-09-001.notes: Ich hätte gern… is a polite way to order: literally 'I would have gladly'. It's slightly more polite than Ich möchte.

DE-A2-09-002.notes: Könnten Sie…? (could you?) is the Konjunktiv II of können and much politer than Können Sie…? The infinitive helfen goes to the end.

DE-A2-09-003.notes: würde + infinitive forms the Konjunktiv II of most verbs: Ich würde gern mitkommen. gern softens it into a wish.

DE-A2-09-004.notes: sein has its own Konjunktiv II, wäre; würde sein is avoided. Das wäre schön = that would be nice. Its past form is wäre … gewesen.

DE-A2-09-005.notes: Würden Sie bitte…? is a polite request; the infinitive goes to the end: schließen. Werden Sie…? would ask about the future instead.

DE-A2-09-006.notes: solltest (Konjunktiv II of sollen) gives advice: you should. It looks like the past (solltest), and context shows which is meant.

DE-A2-10-001.notes: seit + present tense is for something still going on (I've been learning); vor is 'ago' with a past tense; für is a planned period.

DE-A2-10-002.notes: seit takes the dative, and the dative plural adds -n: seit drei Jahren. The verb stays in the present: Ich wohne seit…

DE-A2-10-003.notes: bis means 'until' and is used with times and dates: bis 20 Uhr. With an article it combines with zu: bis zum Abend.

DE-A2-10-004.notes: ab means 'from (starting at)' and looks forward: ab Montag. von … an means the same: von Montag an. ab also gives a starting place: ab Berlin.

DE-A2-10-005.notes: Dates use the ordinal with an adjective ending: der dritte Mai. Ordinals add -te up to 19 (dritte is irregular) and -ste from 20.

DE-A2-10-006.notes: 'On' a date is am + dative ordinal: am ersten Juni. erste is irregular, from eins. In writing it's am 1. Juni.

DE-A2-10-007.notes: Time phrases without a preposition take the accusative: jeden Tag. Tag is masculine, so jeder → jeden.

DE-A2-10-008.notes: letzte Woche is accusative feminine with no preposition. Woche is feminine, so letzte with -e. The masculine would be letzten Monat, the neuter letztes Jahr.

DE-A2-10-009.notes: nächsten Monat is masculine accusative: -en. The phrase takes first position, so ziehen comes second.

DE-A2-10-010.notes: den ganzen Tag (all day) is an accusative of duration. After den, the adjective takes -en. Likewise die ganze Woche, das ganze Jahr.

DE-A2-10-011.notes: Habitual adverbs end in -s and are lower-case: montags (on Mondays). With heute, the time of day is a capitalised noun: heute Abend.

DE-A2-10-012.notes: abends (in the evenings) is lower-case, as an adverb. Likewise morgens, mittags, nachts. Abends would only be capitalised here because it begins the sentence.

DE-A2-10-013.notes: gegen + time means 'around, approximately': gegen acht Uhr. um acht Uhr would be exact. gegen also means 'against' with nouns: gegen den Plan.

DE-A2-10-014.notes: am Wochenende (at the weekend) uses an + dem, like days of the week: am Montag, am Wochenende. Here it takes first position, so the verb schlafe comes straight after.
DE-A2-10-014.tr: At the weekend I have a lie-in.
DE-A2-10-014.flag: dup: replaced Was macht ihr am Wochenende? (near-identical to A1-02-002 Was machst du am Wochenende?); answer am → Am (sentence-initial)

DE-A2-10-015.notes: in der Nacht (in the night) uses in + dative. nachts means 'at night' in general. The same pattern gives in der Woche (during the week).

DE-A2-10-016.notes: zu Weihnachten is the northern form; southern Germany and Austria say an Weihnachten. Both are standard.

DE-A2-10-017.notes: A year alone takes no preposition (2010 bin ich…), or im Jahr 2010. in 2010 is an anglicism. Decades take in: in den Neunzigerjahren.
DE-A2-10-017.tip: Not in 2010: just 2010 or im Jahr 2010.

DE-A2-10-018.notes: noch nichts means 'nothing yet', and noch nicht 'not yet'. The answer to it is schon (already). With a verb in place of nichts, it's noch nicht: Ich habe noch nicht gegessen.

DE-A2-10-019.notes: kein … mehr means 'no more, none left': kein Geld mehr. With a verb it's nicht mehr: Ich kann nicht mehr.

DE-A2-10-020.notes: erst with a number means 'only, no more than': Er ist erst fünf. It implies 'less than you might expect'.

DE-A2-10-021.notes: erst with a time means 'not until': erst um zehn. nur um zehn would be wrong here. In the past it means 'only then': Er kam erst um zehn.
DE-A2-10-021.tip: erst um zehn = not until ten.

DE-A2-10-022.notes: nicht mehr means 'no longer, not any more': Sie wohnt nicht mehr hier. It's the opposite of noch. The word order is nicht mehr, never mehr nicht.

DE-A2-10-023.notes: Sequencing words take first position, so the verb follows straight after: Zuerst kaufen wir…, dann kochen wir… The subject comes third.

DE-A2-10-024.notes: Was für ein …! is an exclamation: what a…! ein declines with the noun: Was für ein schöner Tag (masculine nominative -er).

DE-A2-10-025.notes: Date ranges use von … bis: vom 3. bis 5. Mai. Ordinals are written with a full stop: 3. = dritten. The ordinal after vom and bis zum is in the dative.

DE-A2-10-026.notes: In a letter heading, the date takes den + ordinal: Berlin, den 3. Mai 2026. In emails and modern letters, Berlin, 3. Mai 2026 is also fine.

DE-A2-11-001.notes: Standing alone, ein takes full endings: einen (masculine accusative) for Stift. ein with no ending only appears before a noun.

DE-A2-11-002.notes: Standing alone in the neuter, ein becomes eins (or eines): Da ist eins. Café is neuter. The masculine would be einer: Da ist einer.

DE-A2-11-003.notes: kein standing alone also takes full endings: keins for neuter Auto. keiner (m.) and keine (f.) work the same way.

DE-A2-11-004.notes: welcher (which) declines like der: welchen Film (masculine accusative). It asks about one of a known set.

DE-A2-11-005.notes: jemand (somebody) takes the er form of the verb: Jemand hat angerufen. Its accusative and dative (jemanden, jemandem) are optional in speech.

DE-A2-11-006.notes: niemand (nobody) is negative on its own, so no nicht is needed: Niemand ist zu Hause. Double negatives are wrong.

DE-A2-11-007.notes: nichts (nothing) never changes. It can be the subject, as here, or the object: Ich habe nichts gesehen.
DE-A2-11-007.flag: dup: replaced Ich habe nichts gesehen (near-identical to A2-10-018 Ich habe noch nichts gegessen); answer nichts → Nichts (sentence-initial)

DE-A2-11-008.notes: etwas (something) never changes; in speech it's often shortened to was. In questions it can mean 'anything'.
DE-A2-11-008.flag: dup: replaced Möchtest du etwas trinken? (near-identical to A1-02-028 Was möchtest du trinken?)

DE-A2-11-009.notes: Possessives standing alone take full endings: meiner for masculine Schlüssel. They match the gender of the noun left out.

DE-A2-11-010.notes: Standing alone, the neuter possessive is deins (or deines). Handy is neuter. The masculine is deiner, the feminine deine.

DE-A2-11-011.notes: ihres (hers) is neuter for Auto. The same form also means 'theirs'; context decides. The masculine is ihrer: Mein Hund ist alt, ihrer ist jung.

DE-A2-11-012.notes: In speech, der / die / das are used as stressed pronouns: den kenne ich nicht. They're often fronted for emphasis.

DE-A2-11-013.notes: Die ist sehr nett uses die as a pronoun for die Kollegin. It's neutral in speech; in writing sie is better.

DE-A2-11-014.notes: The demonstrative pronoun in the dative masculine is dem: mit dem. It sounds dismissive here, as often with demonstratives.

DE-A2-12-001.notes: Names add -s with no apostrophe: Annas Auto. An apostrophe (Anna's) is a common anglicism, tolerated on shop signs only.

DE-A2-12-002.notes: In speech, von + dative replaces the genitive: das Auto von meinem Bruder. In writing, the genitive (meines Bruders) is preferred.

DE-A2-12-003.notes: wessen (whose) is the genitive of wer. In speech, Wem gehört die Tasche? is more common. It is followed directly by the noun owned: Wessen Tasche?

DE-A2-12-004.notes: The genitive plural article is der, and possessives take -er: meiner Eltern. The noun itself adds no ending.

DE-A2-13-001.notes: werden + noun means 'become': Ich werde Lehrerin. There's no article with jobs, as with sein. A man would say Ich werde Lehrer.

DE-A2-13-002.notes: es wird dunkel = it's getting dark: werden + adjective describes a change. schon here means 'already'.

DE-A2-13-003.notes: werden + infinitive forms the future: Was wirst du machen? du takes wirst, with no d. In speech, the present with a time word often replaces this future.

DE-A2-13-004.notes: The past of werden is wurde: Er wurde krank (he fell ill). It's also the past passive auxiliary. The Perfekt is ist … geworden.

DE-A2-14-001.notes: Nouns in -heit are always feminine: die Freiheit. Likewise -keit (die Möglichkeit) and -ung. -heit nouns often come from adjectives: frei → die Freiheit.

DE-A2-14-002.notes: Nouns in -um are neuter: das Museum, das Zentrum. Their plural often replaces -um with -en: Museen. montags here means 'on Mondays'.

DE-A2-14-003.notes: Nouns in -ling are masculine: der Frühling, der Lehrling, der Liebling. The other seasons are masculine too: der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter.

DE-A2-14-004.notes: Nouns in -tät are feminine: die Universität, die Qualität. They're mostly Latin loans. The stress falls on the final syllable: Universität.

DE-A2-14-005.notes: Nouns in -ismus are masculine: der Tourismus, der Kapitalismus. The plural is rare; -ismus nouns are mostly uncountable.

DE-A2-14-006.notes: Nouns in -ment are mostly neuter: das Dokument, das Instrument. der Zement is an exception. The plural is -e: Dokumente.

DE-A2-14-007.notes: Nouns in -ion are feminine: die Situation, die Nation, die Information. The plural is -en: Situationen.

DE-A2-14-008.notes: Metals are neuter: das Gold, das Silber, das Eisen. Exceptions include die Bronze and der Stahl. Metal nouns rarely have plurals.

DE-A2-14-009.notes: Numbers used as nouns are feminine: die Eins, die Drei. German school marks run from 1 (best) to 6. eine Eins is the best mark.

DE-A2-14-010.notes: Diminutives in -chen are always neuter, whatever the base noun: die Katze → das Kätzchen. -lein (das Kätzlein) is a more literary equivalent.

DE-A2-14-011.notes: -chen adds an umlaut where possible: Haus → Häuschen. Häuschen also means a little cottage. Diminutives in -chen take no plural ending: zwei Häuschen.

DE-A2-14-012.notes: Tochter forms its plural with an umlaut only: Töchter. Mutter does the same: Mütter. studieren means study at university.

DE-A2-14-013.notes: Nacht takes umlaut + -e: Nächte. Several one-syllable feminines do the same: Stadt → Städte, Hand → Hände.

DE-A2-14-014.notes: Garten ends in -en, so it adds no ending, only an umlaut: Gärten. Masculine nouns in -el behave the same way: Mantel → Mäntel.

DE-A2-14-015.notes: Kino ends in a vowel other than -e, so the plural is -s: Kinos. es gibt takes the accusative but this doesn't show in the plural.
